enrichment.short_title: Employment tribunal preliminary views and apparent bias
key_facts: London Borough of Southwark appealed an Employment Tribunal finding of disability discrimination and constructive unfair dismissal in favour of employee Tony Jiminez.
On 12 March 1999, after nearly all evidence had been heard, the tribunal chairman expressed strongly adverse preliminary views about Southwark's treatment of Mr Jiminez.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal held this showed apparent bias and remitted the case; Mr Jiminez appealed to the Court of Appeal.
The Court of Appeal held the EAT should first have obtained the chairman's comments under the EAT Practice Direction and that no apparent bias was shown.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision setting aside an employment tribunal judgment for apparent bias.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; EAT decision set aside and the employment tribunal decision restored.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employment tribunal, with the parties' consent and after most evidence has been heard, gives trenchant but expressly preliminary views to focus closing submissions, a fair-minded informed observer will not conclude there was a real possibility of bias; failure to follow the EAT Practice Direction procedure for bias complaints is a material error entitling the Court of Appeal to reconsider the issue afresh.
legal_issues: Whether strongly expressed preliminary tribunal views before final submissions amount to apparent bias
Application of the Porter v Magill objective observer test
Procedural requirements under paragraph 9 of the Employment Appeal Tribunal Practice Direction
Distinction between provisional judicial comment and a concluded hostile view

enrichment.short_title: GMC specialist register and family planning specialty

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service (Appointment of Consultants) Regulations 1982

key_facts: Three doctors with extensive experience in family planning and reproductive health care (FPRHC) applied under transitional provisions to be included on the GMC specialist register.
About 70 existing NHS consultants in FPRHC had already been registered by the Registrar under Article 12(2)(a).
STA appeal panels held FPRHC was not a medical specialty and assessed training against obstetrics and gynaecology standards.
Lawrence Collins J dismissed judicial review; the Court of Appeal held the panels adopted the wrong approach to 'specialty' in transitional provisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against refusal of judicial review of Specialist Training Authority appeal panel decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; STA appeal panel decisions quashed and declarations made that each appellant satisfied Article 12(2)(c)(i).
enrichment.ratio: For transitional registration under Article 12 of the 1995 Order, 'specialty' means a field of medicine in which NHS consultants had been appointed before 1997, not a narrowly defined sub-specialty assessed against post-1997 CCST standards; doctors with equivalent FPRHC qualifications should be treated consistently with existing FPRHC consultants already on the register.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'specialty' in Article 12 transitional provisions
Whether FPRHC qualifies as a medical specialty
Relationship between Registrar and STA decision-making under Article 12
Proper assessment of training under Article 12(2)(c)(i)

enrichment.short_title: Council refusal of pension added years after ultra vires compromise

statutes_considered.title: Local Government (Early Termination of Employment) (Discretionary Compensation) (England and Wales) Regulations 2000

key_facts: Mr Foster, former director of environmental services at Eastbourne Borough Council, sought judicial review of the council's refusal to award discretionary pension added years.
An ultra vires compromise agreement had artificially extended his employment past age 50 to secure enhanced retirement benefits.
The Court of Appeal had remitted the case; Mackay J found eligibility gateways open but the council refused added years as irrationally generous.
Mr Justice Moses held awarding added years would have been unlawful because eligibility depended on an artificial unlawful extension of employment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Fourth judicial review hearing on whether Eastbourne Borough Council lawfully refused Regulation 8 added years under the 2000 Discretionary Compensation Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; refusal of added years upheld; permission to appeal refused; council costs of £28,000 agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Added years under the 2000 Regulations are available only where a redundant employee genuinely reached age 50 at termination; a council cannot award added years where continued employment past redundancy was an unlawful artificial extension designed solely to trigger eligibility, even if other enhanced redundancy payments were lawfully made.
legal_issues: Whether added years could lawfully be awarded after an ultra vires compromise agreement
Construction and purpose of Regulation 8 discretionary added years
Effect of prior Court of Appeal findings on continuing employment
Whether Mackay J had found the compromise package irrationally generous

confidence.notes: Long procedural history but core public law issue on added years is clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Post-release licence not a heavier Article 7 penalty
key_facts: Mr Uttley was convicted in 1995 of rape offences committed before 1983 and sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment.
Under pre-1991 law he would have been released unconditionally at two-thirds; under the 1991 Act he must be released on licence until three-quarters.
He claimed the licence conditions and recall risk imposed a heavier penalty contrary to Article 7.
Mr Justice Moses held a post-release licence is preventative and rehabilitative, not a criminal penalty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim that release on licence under the Criminal Justice Act 1991 violated Article 7 ECHR.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Release on licence under section 33 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 is designed to protect the public and assist rehabilitation, not to punish; its restrictive conditions and recall risk do not constitute a heavier 'penalty' within the autonomous meaning of Article 7 even where the offender would previously have been discharged unconditionally at the same point in the sentence.
legal_issues: Autonomous meaning of 'penalty' under Article 7
Whether licence conditions and recall amount to a heavier penalty
Application of Schedule 12 transitional provisions to existing prisoners
Analogy with West v Parole Board on preventative purpose

confidence.notes: Focused first-instance judgment on a defined Article 7 point with clear reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: WRU rugby club promotion assurance and Part 24 strike-out
key_facts: Aberavon and Port Talbot RFC finished first in Welsh Rugby Union Division 1 in 2000/01 but were not promoted after WRU league restructuring.
The club claimed a contractual entitlement to 12 months' notice of league structure changes based on an assurance at a 6 April 1997 special general meeting.
The judge granted summary judgment, holding any such commitment required formal amendment of the WRU constitution under By-law 34.
An amended claim for breach of an implied term not to act capriciously was allowed to proceed to trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against summary judgment under CPR Part 24 striking out a breach-of-assurance claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; summary judgment on the assurance claim upheld, but amended implied-term claim unaffected.
enrichment.ratio: A purported undertaking at an informal WRU special general meeting to give 12 months' notice of league changes, which would fetter the management committee's powers under By-law 12, could only take effect as a constitutional amendment under By-law 34 with the required formalities; such a limitation cannot arise from informal contractual understandings outside the constitution.
legal_issues: Whether an SGM assurance created a binding contractual obligation
Construction of WRU Constitution and By-laws 9, 12 and 34
Proper use of CPR Part 24 on questions of constitutional construction
Whether sporting association rules should be construed informally

enrichment.short_title: ServiceAlliance software contract unpaid fees after termination
key_facts: Astea licensed its ServiceAlliance field-service software to Time Group and agreed configuration, integration and support services in July 2000.
Time stopped paying and put the project on hold in March 2001, claiming Astea's delays were repudiatory; Astea claimed £214,769.14 in unpaid licence fees and services.
The judge found the contract a single composite agreement, Astea performed within a reasonable time, and Time did not accept any repudiation.
Time's Part 20 counterclaim for wasted implementation costs and lost staff savings failed for lack of proof and failure to mitigate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of breach-of-contract and Part 20 counterclaim following non-payment and project termination.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Astea for £214,769.14 plus interest; Time's Part 20 claim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A software licence and implementation services package forming one continuously paginated agreement is a single contract; where the customer suspends the project without accepting repudiation, unpaid licence fees remain due, and a terminating party must permit completion of nearly finished services to mitigate alleged wasted-cost losses.
legal_issues: Whether the ServiceAlliance contract was one agreement or several
Whether Astea repudiated by failing to complete services by March 2001
Whether Time accepted repudiation or merely put the project on hold
Implied term to complete within reasonable time after waiver of 1 August 2000 target
Proof and mitigation of Time's counterclaim losses

enrichment.short_title: Algeria GIA risk and Article 3 on return to Algiers
key_facts: An Algerian post office worker claimed asylum after threats from the GIA and failure of state protection.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal found sufficiency of protection in Algiers and no Convention reason for persecution.
The applicant renewed an application for permission to appeal, arguing Article 3 could be engaged without a Refugee Convention ground.
The Court of Appeal held the tribunal's factual findings on Algiers safety were not arguably wrong and dismissed the application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of leave.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to establish Refugee Convention persecution does not automatically preclude Article 3, but where the tribunal finds sufficiency of state protection against GIA threats in the applicant's home city of Algiers, return engages neither asylum nor Article 3; Mardi does not establish that Algiers is unsafe for relocation.
legal_issues: Whether absence of Refugee Convention grounds precludes Article 3 protection
Sufficiency of protection against non-state GIA violence in Algiers
Whether IAT fact-finding on internal protection was perverse
Distinction from Mardi on relocation to Algerian cities

enrichment.short_title: De facto High Court judge and Article 6 tribunal established by law
key_facts: Mr Coppard sued HMRC for VAT deferment breach; the case was tried by HH Judge Richard Seymour QC.
Judge Seymour was a circuit judge authorised under section 68 for TCC business but lacked a section 9 commission to sit as a High Court judge.
The court enlarged time to appeal and held Judge Seymour was a judge de facto, not a knowing usurper, because he honestly believed TCC appointment sufficed.
The Court of Appeal held the de facto doctrine validates judicial office and complies with Article 6's requirement for a tribunal established by law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on whether an unauthorised TCC judge's High Court judgment was a nullity and incompatible with Article 6.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Judge Seymour's judgment held valid as given by a de facto High Court judge and a tribunal established by law.
enrichment.ratio: The de facto doctrine validates the authority of a judge who honestly but mistakenly believes himself authorised to sit, not a knowing usurper; such a judge-in-fact is established by law for Article 6 purposes because the common law itself confers interim validity to preserve legal certainty, provided the error is formal rather than substantive.
legal_issues: Whether an unsigned section 9 commission renders a TCC judge's High Court judgment a nullity
Scope of the judge de facto doctrine and exclusion of usurpers
Whether de facto validation extends to the office or only to individual acts
Article 6 requirement for a tribunal 'established by law'

confidence.notes: Landmark unanimous constitutional judgment with detailed reasoning on de facto doctrine and Article 6.
